1	// Offline route resolution: match a request against configured route prefixes
2	// and join the remainder onto the upstream base path without any network I/O.
3	package contractsentinel
4	
5	import (
6		"bytes"
7		"encoding/json"
8		"errors"
9		"fmt"
10		"net/netip"
11		"net/url"
12		"sort"
13		"strings"
14	)
15	
16	// Route is one configured route: an id, accepted methods, a path prefix and
17	// the upstream URL requests on that route are forwarded to. An optional
18	// queryTransforms list rewrites the request query string after the route has
19	// been selected.
20	//
21	// QueryTransforms stays tag-less in the default (un)marshal sense: reading
22	// goes through Config.UnmarshalJSON, which decodes each route through the
23	// routeJSON raw mirror and validates the rules before they reach this field,
24	// and writing goes through Route.MarshalJSON, so the rules round-trip
25	// instead of being silently dropped (a plain json:"-" tag only omitted them
26	// on save).
27	type Route struct {
28		ID         string
29		Methods    []string
30		PathPrefix string
31		Upstream   string
32	
33		// QueryTransforms holds the validated rules. When it carries no rules
34		// the field is omitted on save, whether the source named no field or an
35		// explicit queryTransforms: [] — both are valid ways to write a route
36		// without rules, and ParseConfig accepts either.
37		QueryTransforms []*QueryTransform
38	}
39	
40	// pendingRoute is the read-side intermediate form of one route: the decoded
41	// basic fields alongside the still-unchecked raw queryTransforms value. It
42	// exists only inside the config reader, where the rules are validated against
43	// the route's 1-based position in check layer 3, and never becomes part of a
44	// finished Config — Route itself only ever carries the validated result, so
45	// no read path can observe a route that still holds unchecked rule text.
46	type pendingRoute struct {
47		route Route
48		// rawTransforms is the undecoded queryTransforms value, kept apart from
49		// the formal route data until checkQueryTransforms validates it.
50		rawTransforms json.RawMessage
51	}
52	
53	// MarshalJSON writes routes back in the shape ParseConfig accepts: the four
54	// basic fields in their canonical order, followed by queryTransforms when the
55	// route carries rules. A route without rules — whether the source omitted the
56	// field or named queryTransforms: [] — omits it, and ParseConfig accepts
57	// either spelling; the field is never written as null. The rules' order and
58	// literal strings are preserved byte for byte apart from JSON string
59	// escaping, so re-parsing the output and resolving yields the same routeId
60	// and upstreamURL.
61	func (r Route) MarshalJSON() ([]byte, error) {
62		type routeOut struct {
63			ID              string            `json:"id"`
64			Methods         []string          `json:"methods"`
65			PathPrefix      string            `json:"pathPrefix"`
66			Upstream        string            `json:"upstream"`
67			QueryTransforms []*QueryTransform `json:"queryTransforms,omitempty"`
68		}
69		return json.Marshal(routeOut{
70			ID:              r.ID,
71			Methods:         r.Methods,
72			PathPrefix:      r.PathPrefix,
73			Upstream:        r.Upstream,
74			QueryTransforms: r.QueryTransforms,
75		})
76	}
77	
78	// QueryTransform is one rule in a route's queryTransforms array: op is
79	// "set", "remove", "rename" or "copy"; name is matched against decoded
80	// parameter names, value (set only) is used literally, and to (rename and
81	// copy only) is the literal replacement or copy name.
82	type QueryTransform struct {
83		Op    string `json:"op"`
84		Name  string `json:"name"`
85		Value string `json:"value"`
86		To    string `json:"to"`
87	}
88	
89	// queryTransformShapes is the one description of each op's rule grammar,
90	// consulted by both sides of a save: parseQueryTransforms validates a rule
91	// against its entry and QueryTransform.MarshalJSON writes exactly that
92	// shape. The entry names the single field each op owns besides op and name:
93	//
94	//   - "value" (set): required and a JSON string, the empty string included;
95	//   - "to" (rename and copy): required and a non-empty JSON string;
96	//   - "" (remove): neither field is owned.
97	//
98	// Every op that does not own "value" must not carry one, so the read-side
99	// ban and the save-side omission live behind this one table. Fields an op
100	// does not own — a "to" arriving on set or remove, and any unknown key —
101	// stay accepted and ignored on read and are dropped on save just as before;
102	// the table describes the owned fields only and never tightens the grammar.
103	// Rename and copy share one "to" entry, so their target-name requirement
104	// and their ban on "value" cannot be maintained or drift in two places.
105	var queryTransformShapes = map[string]string{
106		"set":    "value",
107		"remove": "",
108		"rename": "to",
109		"copy":   "to",
110	}
111	
112	// MarshalJSON renders each rule in the exact shape queryTransformShapes
113	// pins for input, so the save shape can never drift from the read-side
114	// field requirements:
115	//   - set keeps "value" as a JSON string, including the empty string;
116	//   - remove emits only op and name (never value or to);
117	//   - rename and copy keep "to" and never emit value.
118	//
119	// name, value and to are written as the literal strings read in — spaces,
120	// non-ASCII letters, '+' and '%' included — with only JSON string escaping,
121	// never query-string percent-encoding or decoding, so a re-read matches the
122	// same parameter names and applies the same literal values. An op absent
123	// from the table (one no validated config can carry) renders the
124	// remove-shaped pair and so can never gain a field the reader rejects.
125	func (q *QueryTransform) MarshalJSON() ([]byte, error) {
126		switch queryTransformShapes[q.Op] {
127		case "value":
128			return json.Marshal(struct {
129				Op    string `json:"op"`
130				Name  string `json:"name"`
131				Value string `json:"value"`
132			}{q.Op, q.Name, q.Value})
133		case "to":
134			return json.Marshal(struct {
135				Op   string `json:"op"`
136				Name string `json:"name"`
137				To   string `json:"to"`
138			}{q.Op, q.Name, q.To})
139		default:
140			return json.Marshal(struct {
141				Op   string `json:"op"`
142				Name string `json:"name"`
143			}{q.Op, q.Name})
144		}
145	}
146	
147	// checkRuleFields validates the op-owned field named by queryTransformShapes
148	// for one rule whose op and name are already decoded. set's "value" must be
149	// present as a JSON string (the empty string included); rename/copy's "to"
150	// must be present as a non-empty string; and an op that does not own
151	// "value" must not carry one. The value ban is decided before the owned
152	// field's presence/type, so a rename or copy carrying both keeps failing on
153	// the stray value first. Fields the op does not own stay untouched: a "to"
154	// on set or remove is neither rejected nor copied onto the rule, and saving
155	// omits it. Every reason keeps parseQueryTransforms' existing wording.
156	func checkRuleFields(qt *QueryTransform, ownedField string, fields map[string]json.RawMessage, ruleLoc string) *Failure {
157		valueRaw, hasValue := fields["value"]
158		if ownedField != "value" && hasValue {
159			return failuref("invalid_config", "%s: %s must not include a value", ruleLoc, qt.Op)
160		}
161		switch ownedField {
162		case "value":
163			if !hasValue {
164				return failuref("invalid_config", "%s: %s requires a string value", ruleLoc, qt.Op)
165			}
166			if !jsonString(valueRaw, &qt.Value) {
167				return failuref("invalid_config", "%s: value must be a string", ruleLoc)
168			}
169		case "to":
170			toRaw, hasTo := fields["to"]
171			switch {
172			case !hasTo:
173				return failuref("invalid_config", "%s: %s requires a non-empty string to", ruleLoc, qt.Op)
174			case !jsonString(toRaw, &qt.To):
175				return failuref("invalid_config", "%s: to must be a non-empty string", ruleLoc)
176			case qt.To == "":
177				return failuref("invalid_config", "%s: to must be a non-empty string", ruleLoc)
178			}
179		}
180		return nil
181	}
182	
183	// routeJSON mirrors Route but keeps every field raw: the basic fields are
184	// type-checked by decodeRoute with the route's position (and, when available,
185	// its id), so a wrong field type is reported on that route rather than as a
186	// generic JSON decode error, and queryTransforms can surface null, wrong
187	// types and malformed rules the same way.
188	type routeJSON struct {
189		ID              json.RawMessage `json:"id"`
190		Methods         json.RawMessage `json:"methods"`
191		PathPrefix      json.RawMessage `json:"pathPrefix"`
192		Upstream        json.RawMessage `json:"upstream"`
193		QueryTransforms json.RawMessage `json:"queryTransforms"`
194	}
195	
196	// decodeRoute type-checks and decodes one raw route object into its
197	// intermediate form: the basic fields land on the pending route, while the
198	// raw queryTransforms value travels alongside it, still unchecked, for check
199	// layer 3. loc is the route's 1-based location in its config (e.g.
200	// "route 2"). The element's JSON type is checked first: a null entry or any
201	// non-object value fails on the entry itself, naming the position, the
202	// required object type and the type actually received, instead of falling
203	// through to a missing-field error such as a missing id. Field type errors
204	// then carry that location and, when the route supplies a valid non-empty
205	// string id anywhere in its object (even after the offending field), that id.
206	// Missing fields stay silent here and are rejected later by validate, which
207	// preserves the existing missing-field behavior.
208	func decodeRoute(data []byte, loc string) (pendingRoute, *Failure) {
209		elem := bytes.TrimSpace(data)
210		if len(elem) == 0 || elem[0] != '{' {
211			return pendingRoute{}, failuref("invalid_config",
212				"%s: route entry must be an object, got %s", loc, jsonTypeName(elem))
213		}
214		var rj routeJSON
215		if err := json.Unmarshal(elem, &rj); err != nil {
216			// The element already parsed as one JSON value and starts with '{';
217			// an object that cannot be read is a syntax failure rather than a
218			// field type error.
219			return pendingRoute{}, failuref("invalid_config", "config is not valid JSON: %v", err)
220		}
221	
222		var pending pendingRoute
223		route := &pending.route
224		// Type-check id first so it can identify the route on an error in any
225		// later field regardless of object order. Only a valid non-empty JSON
226		// string becomes the label; a wrong-typed id is reported against the id
227		// field and never rendered (e.g. as a number or object) as the route's
228		// identity, so that error is located by position alone.
229		if !decodeStringField(rj.ID, &route.ID) {
230			return pendingRoute{}, failuref("invalid_config", "%s: id must be a string", loc)
231		}
232		label := loc
233		if route.ID != "" {
234			label = routeLabel(loc, route.ID)
235		}
236	
237		if f := decodeMethodsField(rj.Methods, label, &route.Methods); f != nil {
238			return pendingRoute{}, f
239		}
240		if f := decodeRouteStringField(rj.PathPrefix, label, "pathPrefix", &route.PathPrefix); f != nil {
241			return pendingRoute{}, f
242		}
243		if f := decodeRouteStringField(rj.Upstream, label, "upstream", &route.Upstream); f != nil {
244			return pendingRoute{}, f
245		}
246		pending.rawTransforms = rj.QueryTransforms
247		return pending, nil
248	}
249	
250	// decodeRouteStringField renders a route field's string type error with the
251	// route's position (and, when available, its id); the type decision itself is
252	// the shared decodeStringField. An absent field stays silent for the later
253	// required-field validation.
254	func decodeRouteStringField(raw json.RawMessage, label, field string, dst *string) *Failure {
255		if !decodeStringField(raw, dst) {
256			return failuref("invalid_config", "%s: %s must be a string", label, field)
257		}
258		return nil
259	}
260	
261	// decodeStringField type-checks a raw field that must hold a string. It is
262	// the one shared string-field decision used by both config and request
263	// decoding, so the absent / null / non-string / empty-string distinctions
264	// live in one place. It returns false only when the key is present with a
265	// non-string value (null included), which is always a field type error. An
266	// absent key leaves dst untouched, and a present string — the empty string
267	// included — is decoded into dst, so both reach the existing content checks
268	// unchanged.
269	func decodeStringField(raw json.RawMessage, dst *string) (isString bool) {
270		if len(raw) == 0 {
271			return true
272		}
273		return jsonString(raw, dst)
274	}
275	
276	// decodeMethodsField type-checks methods: it must be an array of strings
277	// when present. An absent field is left nil for later required-field
278	// validation; null or any non-array value fails the field, and a number,
279	// boolean, object or null entry fails with the offending entry's position.
280	func decodeMethodsField(raw json.RawMessage, label string, dst *[]string) *Failure {
281		if len(raw) == 0 {
282			return nil
283		}
284		body := bytes.TrimSpace(raw)
285		if string(body) == "null" || len(body) == 0 || body[0] != '[' {
286			return failuref("invalid_config", "%s: methods must be an array of strings", label)
287		}
288		var elems []json.RawMessage
289		if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &elems); err != nil {
290			return failuref("invalid_config", "%s: methods must be an array of strings", label)
291		}
292		methods := make([]string, 0, len(elems))
293		for i, elem := range elems {
294			var m string
295			if !jsonString(bytes.TrimSpace(elem), &m) {
296				return failuref("invalid_config", "%s: methods entry %d must be a string", label, i+1)
297			}
298			methods = append(methods, m)
299		}
300		*dst = methods
301		return nil
302	}
303	
304	// parseQueryTransforms decodes and validates the raw queryTransforms array
305	// of one route. loc identifies the route; rule errors additionally carry a
306	// 1-based rule index.
307	func parseQueryTransforms(raw json.RawMessage, loc, id string) ([]*QueryTransform, *Failure) {
308		body := strings.TrimSpace(string(raw))
309		if body == "null" {
310			return nil, failuref("invalid_config", "%s: queryTransforms must not be null", routeLabel(loc, id))
311		}
312		var elems []json.RawMessage
313		if err := json.Unmarshal([]byte(body), &elems); err != nil {
314			return nil, failuref("invalid_config", "%s: queryTransforms must be an array", routeLabel(loc, id))
315		}
316		transforms := make([]*QueryTransform, 0, len(elems))
317		for i, elem := range elems {
318			ruleLoc := fmt.Sprintf("%s, queryTransforms rule %d", routeLabel(loc, id), i+1)
319			if string(bytes.TrimSpace(elem)) == "null" {
320				return nil, failuref("invalid_config", "%s: rule must not be null", ruleLoc)
321			}
322			var fields map[string]json.RawMessage
323			if err := json.Unmarshal(elem, &fields); err != nil {
324				return nil, failuref("invalid_config", "%s: rule must be a JSON object", ruleLoc)
325			}
326	
327			qt := &QueryTransform{}
328			opRaw, ok := fields["op"]
329			switch {
330			case !ok:
331				return nil, failuref("invalid_config", "%s: op is required", ruleLoc)
332			case !jsonString(opRaw, &qt.Op):
333				return nil, failuref("invalid_config", "%s: op must be a string", ruleLoc)
334			}
335			// The op decides the rule's shape once, through the same
336			// queryTransformShapes table the saver uses; an unknown op fails
337			// before name so it never reaches a field requirement.
338			ownedField, knownOp := queryTransformShapes[qt.Op]
339			if !knownOp {
340				return nil, failuref("invalid_config", "%s: unknown op %q (only set, remove, rename and copy are supported)", ruleLoc, qt.Op)
341			}
342	
343			nameRaw, ok := fields["name"]
344			switch {
345			case !ok:
346				return nil, failuref("invalid_config", "%s: name is required", ruleLoc)
347			case !jsonString(nameRaw, &qt.Name):
348				return nil, failuref("invalid_config", "%s: name must be a non-empty string", ruleLoc)
349			case qt.Name == "":
350				return nil, failuref("invalid_config", "%s: name must be a non-empty string", ruleLoc)
351			}
352	
353			if f := checkRuleFields(qt, ownedField, fields, ruleLoc); f != nil {
354				return nil, f
355			}
356			transforms = append(transforms, qt)
357		}
358		return transforms, nil
359	}
360	
361	// jsonString decodes raw into s and reports whether raw is a JSON string
362	// (null, numbers, objects and arrays fail).
363	func jsonString(raw json.RawMessage, s *string) bool {
364		if len(raw) == 0 || raw[0] != '"' {
365			return false
366		}
367		return json.Unmarshal(raw, s) == nil
368	}
369	
370	// routeLabel renders the human-readable route location, adding the id when
371	// the configuration supplied one.
372	func routeLabel(loc, id string) string {
373		if id != "" {
374			return fmt.Sprintf("%s (id %q)", loc, id)
375		}
376		return loc
377	}
378	
379	// Config is the resolve configuration: a flat array of routes.
380	type Config struct {
381		Routes []Route `json:"routes"`
382	}
383	
384	// MarshalJSON writes the config back in the shape ParseConfig accepts. A
385	// non-nil empty (or nil) routes slice is emitted as "routes": [] rather than
386	// "routes": null, which ParseConfig would reject with invalid_config; the
387	// routes keep their parsed order and each route marshals through
388	// Route.MarshalJSON so its queryTransforms survive the save.
389	func (cfg *Config) MarshalJSON() ([]byte, error) {
390		routes := cfg.Routes
391		if routes == nil {
392			routes = []Route{}
393		}
394		return json.Marshal(struct {
395			Routes []Route `json:"routes"`
396		}{Routes: routes})
397	}
398	
399	// UnmarshalJSON runs check layers 1–3 of config reading (see ParseConfig for
400	// the full layer list and the error-selection rules): JSON syntax, then the
401	// document structure and basic field types, then the queryTransforms rules.
402	// Layer 4 (field contents) is Config.validate, run by ParseConfig after
403	// decoding. The routes are decoded one entry at a time from raw values, each
404	// type-checked against its 1-based position in this config, so a wrong field
405	// type is reported on the offending route (with its id when available)
406	// instead of as a generic JSON syntax failure, and configs parsed
407	// concurrently or interleaved in the same process cannot shift each other's
408	// route numbering. A broken JSON document fails the outer decode and is
409	// reported as a parse failure, without a guessed route position or field.
410	func (cfg *Config) UnmarshalJSON(data []byte) error {
411		read, err := readConfig(data)
412		if err != nil {
413			return err
414		}
415		*cfg = *read
416		return nil
417	}
418	
419	// readConfig runs check layers 1–3 and returns the configuration with every
420	// route's basic fields decoded and its queryTransforms validated. The
421	// intermediate pendingRoutes keep the unchecked rule text out of the
422	// returned Config; layer 4 (field contents) is Config.validate, run by
423	// ParseConfig.
424	func readConfig(data []byte) (*Config, error) {
425		// Layer 1: JSON syntax. A broken document is only ever a parse failure,
426		// reported without a guessed route position or field.
427		body, err := unmarshalJSONValue(data)
428		if err != nil {
429			return nil, err
430		}
431		// Layer 2: structure and basic field types.
432		if f := requireJSONObject(body, "invalid_config", "config", true); f != nil {
433			return nil, f
434		}
435		routes, err := decodeConfigRoutes(body)
436		if err != nil {
437			return nil, err
438		}
439		// Layer 3: query rewrite rules, checked only once every route's basic
440		// fields have the right type, so a type error on any route — earlier or
441		// later — is always reported before any rule error.
442		if f := checkQueryTransforms(routes); f != nil {
443			return nil, f
444		}
445		cfg := &Config{Routes: make([]Route, len(routes))}
446		for i := range routes {
447			cfg.Routes[i] = routes[i].route
448		}
449		return cfg, nil
450	}
451	
452	// decodeConfigRoutes is check layer 2: the top-level object is taken apart
453	// and every route entry is type-checked against its 1-based position. The
454	// routes field must hold an array when present — null is a type error here,
455	// never an absent field: a config that explicitly supplies routes must supply
456	// an array. A non-object entry (null included) fails on that entry before
457	// any field is inspected, and a wrong field type is reported on the offending
458	// route with its id when the route supplies a valid non-empty string id
459	// anywhere in its object. Each route's unchecked queryTransforms value
460	// travels in the returned pendingRoutes for layer 3.
461	func decodeConfigRoutes(body json.RawMessage) ([]pendingRoute, error) {
462		var fields map[string]json.RawMessage
463		if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &fields); err != nil {
464			return nil, err
465		}
466	
467		var rawRoutes []json.RawMessage
468		if raw, ok := fields["routes"]; ok {
469			elem := bytes.TrimSpace(raw)
470			if len(elem) == 0 || elem[0] != '[' {
471				return nil, failuref("invalid_config", "routes must be an array, got %s", jsonTypeName(elem))
472			}
473			if err := json.Unmarshal(elem, &rawRoutes); err != nil {
474				return nil, err
475			}
476		}
477	
478		routes := make([]pendingRoute, len(rawRoutes))
479		for i, entry := range rawRoutes {
480			route, f := decodeRoute(entry, fmt.Sprintf("route %d", i+1))
481			if f != nil {
482				return nil, f
483			}
484			routes[i] = route
485		}
486		return routes, nil
487	}
488	
489	// checkQueryTransforms is check layer 3: every route's raw queryTransforms
490	// value is decoded and validated against the route's 1-based position, in
491	// routes-array order, and the validated rules replace the pending raw value.
492	// It runs only after layer 2 has cleared every route, so a basic-field type
493	// error on any route — earlier or later — is always reported before any rule
494	// error, while within this layer the earliest route (and within it the
495	// earliest rule) wins.
496	func checkQueryTransforms(routes []pendingRoute) *Failure {
497		for i := range routes {
498			if len(routes[i].rawTransforms) == 0 {
499				continue // field absent
500			}
501			loc := fmt.Sprintf("route %d", i+1)
502			transforms, f := parseQueryTransforms(routes[i].rawTransforms, loc, routes[i].route.ID)
503			if f != nil {
504				return f
505			}
506			routes[i].route.QueryTransforms = transforms
507			routes[i].rawTransforms = nil
508		}
509		return nil
510	}
511	
512	// unmarshalJSONValue is the shared first step of parsing either input: it
513	// confirms the document is one syntactically valid JSON value, without
514	// judging its shape. It returns encoding/json's own error verbatim, so each
515	// caller keeps its existing handling (ParseConfig wraps a returned error just
516	// as Config.UnmarshalJSON returning it directly always has).
517	func unmarshalJSONValue(data []byte) (json.RawMessage, error) {
518		var doc json.RawMessage
519		if err := json.Unmarshal(data, &doc); err != nil {
520			return nil, err
521		}
522		return bytes.TrimSpace(doc), nil
523	}
524	
525	// requireJSONObject is the shared top-level shape check: a syntactically
526	// legal value that is not a JSON object is a structural error in the caller's
527	// code saying "<what> must be a JSON object", never a parse failure and never
528	// a guessed field or route position. Config errors additionally name the type
529	// actually received ("got <type>"); the request wording omits it.
530	func requireJSONObject(doc json.RawMessage, code, what string, nameType bool) *Failure {
531		if len(doc) == 0 || doc[0] != '{' {
532			if nameType {
533				return failuref(code, "%s must be a JSON object, got %s", what, jsonTypeName(doc))
534			}
535			return failuref(code, "%s must be a JSON object", what)
536		}
537		return nil
538	}

540	// Request is one resolution request: an HTTP method and a request target
541	// (path with an optional raw query string).
542	type Request struct {
543		Method string `json:"method"`
544		Target string `json:"target"`
545	}
546	
547	// Resolution is the successful result of matching a request.
548	type Resolution struct {
549		RouteID     string `json:"routeId"`
550		UpstreamURL string `json:"upstreamURL"`
551	}
552	
553	// Failure carries a stable machine-readable code and a human-readable reason.
554	type Failure struct {
555		Code       string   `json:"code"`
556		Reason     string   `json:"reason"`
557		Candidates []string `json:"candidates,omitempty"`
558	}
559	
560	func (f *Failure) Error() string { return f.Code + ": " + f.Reason }
561	
562	func failuref(code, format string, args ...any) *Failure {
563		return &Failure{Code: code, Reason: fmt.Sprintf(format, args...)}
564	}
565	
566	// ParseConfig parses and fully validates the route configuration. Reading
567	// checks the document in four layers, and the first layer that finds a
568	// problem decides which error is reported:
569	//
570	//  1. JSON syntax: a broken document is only ever a parse failure, reported
571	//     without a guessed route position or field.
572	//  2. Structure and basic field types: the top-level value must be an
573	//     object, routes must be an array of objects, and id, methods,
574	//     pathPrefix and upstream must carry their JSON types.
575	//  3. Query rewrite rules: each route's queryTransforms array and every rule
576	//     in it.
577	//  4. Field contents: a non-empty unique id, legal methods, an absolute
578	//     pathPrefix (with no direct space, C0 control byte or DEL — only
579	//     percent encoding may carry those) and a valid upstream
580	//     (Config.validate).
581	//
582	// Within one layer the earliest array position wins — routes by their
583	// position in the routes array and rules by their position in the route's
584	// queryTransforms array, never by id ordering or by the object field order.
585	// Layers 1–3 run in Config.UnmarshalJSON (so they also guard a plain
586	// json.Unmarshal into a Config); layer 4 runs here, after decoding. Every
587	// failure hands back no config at all, so a half-parsed configuration can
588	// never resolve a request.
589	func ParseConfig(data []byte) (*Config, *Failure) {
590		var cfg Config
591		if err := json.Unmarshal(data, &cfg); err != nil {
592			if f, ok := err.(*Failure); ok {
593				return nil, f
594			}
595			return nil, failuref("invalid_config", "config is not valid JSON: %v", err)
596		}
597		if f := cfg.validate(); f != nil {
598			return nil, f
599		}
600		return &cfg, nil
601	}
602	
603	// validate is check layer 4 (see ParseConfig): the field contents of every
604	// route, in routes-array order. It runs only after layers 1–3 have cleared
605	// the whole document, so any structure, field-type or rule error anywhere is
606	// reported before any content error.
607	func (cfg *Config) validate() *Failure {
608		seenIDs := make(map[string]int, len(cfg.Routes))
609		for i := range cfg.Routes {
610			route := &cfg.Routes[i]
611			loc := fmt.Sprintf("route %d", i+1)
612			if route.ID == "" {
613				return failuref("invalid_config", "%s: id must be non-empty", loc)
614			}
615			if first, ok := seenIDs[route.ID]; ok {
616				return failuref("invalid_config", "%s: duplicate id %q (already used by route %d)", loc, route.ID, first)
617			}
618			seenIDs[route.ID] = i + 1
619	
620			if len(route.Methods) == 0 {
621				return failuref("invalid_config", "%s (id %q): methods must be a non-empty array", loc, route.ID)
622			}
623			for _, method := range route.Methods {
624				switch {
625				case method == "":
626					return failuref("invalid_config", "%s (id %q): methods must not contain empty entries", loc, route.ID)
627				case method == "*":
628					// Wildcard matching any legal method.
629				case !isToken(method):
630					return failuref("invalid_config", "%s (id %q): invalid method %q", loc, route.ID, method)
631				}
632			}
633	
634			if f := validatePrefix(route.PathPrefix, loc, route.ID); f != nil {
635				return f
636			}
637			if f := validateUpstream(route.Upstream, loc, route.ID); f != nil {
638				return f
639			}
640		}
641		return nil
642	}
643	
644	func validatePrefix(prefix, loc, id string) *Failure {
645		switch {
646		case prefix == "" || prefix[0] != '/':
647			return failuref("invalid_config", "%s (id %q): pathPrefix must start with /", loc, id)
648		case prefix != "/" && strings.HasSuffix(prefix, "/"):
649			return failuref("invalid_config", "%s (id %q): pathPrefix must not end with / except for root", loc, id)
650		case strings.ContainsAny(prefix, "?#"):
651			return failuref("invalid_config", "%s (id %q): pathPrefix must not contain a query string or fragment", loc, id)
652		case !validPercentEscapes(prefix):
653			return failuref("invalid_config", "%s (id %q): pathPrefix contains an invalid percent escape", loc, id)
654		}
655		if f := validatePrefixDirectCharacters(prefix, loc, id); f != nil {
656			return f
657		}
658		return nil
659	}

661	// validatePrefixDirectCharacters rejects a direct space or control byte in a
662	// pathPrefix: a direct ASCII space (U+0020), a C0 control byte (U+0000
663	// through U+001F) or DEL (U+007F) makes the whole configuration
664	// invalid_config, because a request target can never carry that character
665	// directly — ParseRequest rejects it before route selection — so such a
666	// prefix could never be hit by a legal request. The check is decided on the
667	// decoded configured string: writing the byte literally or spelling it as a
668	// JSON escape ("\n", "\t", or the backslash-u0020 space escape) decodes to
669	// the same byte and fails
670	// the same way. Bytes inside a well-formed percent escape are skipped
671	// without decoding, so "%20", "%09" and "%00" stay legal raw text and keep
672	// matching on the raw encoded form; the prefix is never trimmed, the byte is
673	// never stripped or percent-encoded on the user's behalf, and the rule is
674	// not widened to other Unicode content (e.g. Chinese characters). It runs in
675	// check layer 4 (Config.validate), after JSON syntax, structure and basic
676	// field types and the queryTransforms rules, in routes-array order like the
677	// other field-content checks, so a later route's bad queryTransforms rule or
678	// an earlier route's other content error keeps its existing precedence. The
679	// reason names the pathPrefix field, the route's 1-based position and valid
680	// non-empty id and the first offending character as U+XXXX.
681	func validatePrefixDirectCharacters(prefix, loc, id string) *Failure {
682		if c, ok := firstDirectRawCharacter(prefix); ok {
683			return failuref("invalid_config",
684				"%s (id %q): pathPrefix contains a character that must be percent-encoded: U+%04X is not allowed to appear directly in a pathPrefix (a request target may not carry it directly either, so no legal request could match this route; percent-encode it, e.g. %%20 for a space; the prefix is used exactly as configured and the byte is never stripped, trimmed or encoded on its behalf)",
685				loc, id, c)
686		}
687		return nil
688	}

690	// upstreamParts is the one shared reading of a raw upstream URL's address
691	// boundaries. Every field is a slice of the original bytes (nothing is
692	// copied, decoded or normalized), so validation and joining cannot disagree
693	// about where one part ends and the next begins:
694	//
695	//	scheme "://" [userinfo "@"] hostPort basePath
696	//
697	// authority runs from after "://" to the first path slash, and hostPort is
698	// the authority after its last '@', so colons in userinfo or the base path
699	// can never be read as part of an IPv6 host, while brackets, a port and a
700	// zone stay inside hostPort.
701	type upstreamParts struct {
702		raw       string // the upstream exactly as configured; every other field slices this
703		schemeEnd int    // index of the ':' in "://", or -1 when the scheme is absent
704		authority string // bytes between "://" and the first path slash (userinfo included)
705		hostPort  string // authority after the last '@' (host plus optional port)
706		basePath  string // from the first path slash to the end, or ""
707	}
708	
709	// splitUpstream applies the single boundary rule shared by the bracketed-host
710	// check, the unbracketed-IPv6 check and the final join. It never rejects
711	// anything on its own: a raw value without "://" comes back with schemeEnd
712	// set to -1 and empty parts, leaving the generic absolute-URL check to
713	// report it, exactly as the per-caller preamble used to.
714	func splitUpstream(raw string) upstreamParts {
715		p := upstreamParts{raw: raw, schemeEnd: -1}
716		i := strings.Index(raw, "://")
717		if i < 0 {
718			return p
719		}
720		p.schemeEnd = i
721		tail := raw[i+3:]
722		if j := strings.IndexByte(tail, '/'); j >= 0 {
723			p.authority = tail[:j]
724			p.basePath = tail[j:]
725		} else {
726			p.authority = tail
727		}
728		// Any userinfo precedes the host and ends at the last '@'; that boundary
729		// is what keeps a userinfo colon out of the IPv6-host checks.
730		p.hostPort = p.authority
731		if k := strings.LastIndexByte(p.authority, '@'); k >= 0 {
732			p.hostPort = p.authority[k+1:]
733		}
734		return p
735	}

737	// redactUpstreamUserinfo rewrites a raw upstream address for diagnostic
738	// output: when the authority carries userinfo, the whole userinfo segment —
739	// the username and the optional password, exactly as written, colons and
740	// percent escapes included — is replaced by "***" while the '@' separating
741	// it from the host is kept, so "https://user:p%40ss@:8443/v1" is reported
742	// as "https://***@:8443/v1". The segment is never decoded and never
743	// partially kept: a username-only userinfo, an empty password and a
744	// password carrying colons or percent escapes are all hidden whole. The
745	// userinfo range follows the address's own splitUpstream boundaries —
746	// everything before the last '@' of the authority (the part between "://"
747	// and the first path slash) — so an '@' in the base path is never treated
748	// as userinfo. An address without userinfo, or without a scheme and
749	// authority at all, is returned unchanged, so existing diagnostics keep
750	// their current text.
751	func redactUpstreamUserinfo(raw string) string {
752		p := splitUpstream(raw)
753		if p.schemeEnd < 0 {
754			return raw
755		}
756		k := strings.LastIndexByte(p.authority, '@')
757		if k < 0 {
758			return raw
759		}
760		start := p.schemeEnd + 3
761		return raw[:start] + "***" + raw[start+k:]
762	}

764	// redactURLError renders a url.Parse failure for diagnostic output with the
765	// address's userinfo hidden: url.Error quotes the full original address,
766	// credentials included, so the address is re-rendered through
767	// redactUpstreamUserinfo while the underlying reason (a bad port, an
768	// invalid host escape, an invalid path escape, ...) is kept verbatim. The
769	// one exception is an EscapeError produced while unescaping the userinfo —
770	// its text repeats the malformed credential fragment (e.g. invalid URL
771	// escape "%zz" for a password "%zz") — which urlEscapeErrorFromUserinfo
772	// identifies exactly; that fragment is swapped for a fixed, fragment-free
773	// phrase. A fragment from the host or base path is kept exactly as before,
774	// and the address is never repeated in its original form. Non-url errors
775	// are returned unchanged.
776	func redactURLError(err error) string {
777		var urlErr *url.Error
778		if errors.As(err, &urlErr) {
779			inner := urlErr.Err.Error()
780			if urlEscapeErrorFromUserinfo(urlErr.URL, err) {
781				inner = "invalid URL escape in upstream userinfo (username or password hidden)"
782			}
783			return fmt.Sprintf("parse %q: %s", redactUpstreamUserinfo(urlErr.URL), inner)
784		}
785		return err.Error()
786	}
787	
788	// urlEscapeErrorFromUserinfo reports whether parseErr is the *url.Error a
789	// url.Parse of rawURL failed with because a percent escape inside its
790	// userinfo (the username or optional password between "://" and the
791	// authority's last '@') is malformed. It replays net/url's parseAuthority
792	// ordering exactly — host, then userinfo, then the base path — instead of
793	// searching the reported fragment as a substring, which a truncated
794	// fragment such as "%" or "%4" would match inside otherwise-legal escapes.
795	//
796	// The scheme is not judged here: credential redaction applies to every
797	// scheme, so a non-http address with a bad userinfo escape never quotes
798	// the credential fragment either; callers that only own the http/https
799	// dedicated reason (invalidUpstreamUserinfoEscape) gate on the scheme
800	// themselves. The probe follows the address's own splitUpstream boundaries
801	// and requires userinfo:
802	//
803	//  1. parseErr must wrap url.EscapeError, the only error unescaping the
804	//     username/password (encodeUserPassword mode) produces;
805	//  2. the host, parsed on its own with the same scheme, must succeed —
806	//     parseAuthority unescapes the host first, so any host-side failure
807	//     (a host escape, a bad port or an IP-literal error) is the message
808	//     url.Parse actually reports and keeps its existing wording;
809	//  3. the userinfo is then parsed against a known-good host; the error its
810	//     unescaping produces must be the very same EscapeError reported, so
811	//     the decision cannot fire on a coincidentally equal fragment located
812	//     elsewhere (the grammar check validUserinfo runs first is covered: it
813	//     yields "net/url: invalid userinfo", never an EscapeError).
814	//
815	// The base path is never probed: after a clean host and a failing userinfo
816	// parseAuthority has already returned, before setPath ever runs, so a path
817	// escape cannot be the source even when it spells the same three bytes.
818	func urlEscapeErrorFromUserinfo(rawURL string, parseErr error) bool {
819		var urlErr *url.Error
820		if !errors.As(parseErr, &urlErr) {
821			return false
822		}
823		var reported url.EscapeError
824		if !errors.As(urlErr.Err, &reported) {
825			return false
826		}
827		p := splitUpstream(rawURL)
828		if p.schemeEnd < 0 {
829			return false
830		}
831		k := strings.LastIndexByte(p.authority, '@')
832		if k < 0 {
833			return false // no userinfo: host and base-path escapes keep their wording
834		}
835		// Stage 1 of parseAuthority: the host alone, with the same scheme.
836		if _, err := url.Parse(rawURL[:p.schemeEnd+3] + p.hostPort); err != nil {
837			return false
838		}
839		// Stage 2: replay the userinfo stage against a trivially legal host;
840		// its path is "/", so the only possible failure is the credential's.
841		probe := rawURL[:p.schemeEnd+3] + p.authority[:k] + "@userinfo-escape-probe.invalid/"
842		_, probeErr := url.Parse(probe)
843		if probeErr == nil {
844			return false
845		}
846		var probeURLErr *url.Error
847		if !errors.As(probeErr, &probeURLErr) {
848			return false
849		}
850		var probeEscape url.EscapeError
851		return errors.As(probeURLErr.Err, &probeEscape) && probeEscape.Error() == reported.Error()
852	}
853	
854	// invalidUpstreamUserinfoEscape turns a url.Parse failure attributed to the
855	// userinfo (per urlEscapeErrorFromUserinfo) of an http or https upstream
856	// into the config reader's own content error: the reason names the route's
857	// 1-based position, its id and the upstream field, shows the address with
858	// the whole username and optional password replaced by "***" (the '@' and
859	// the host, port and base path kept), and never repeats the malformed
860	// fragment or any other credential byte. A non-http scheme returns nil so
861	// it keeps the generic parse diagnostic; that path renders through
862	// redactURLError, which still hides the credential fragment, it merely
863	// keeps the standard "not a valid URL" wording rather than this one. Any
864	// other url.Parse failure returns nil for the same reason.
865	func invalidUpstreamUserinfoEscape(raw string, parseErr error, loc, id string) *Failure {
866		if !urlEscapeErrorFromUserinfo(raw, parseErr) {
867			return nil
868		}
869		// The dedicated, field-located reason is the http/https contract; other
870		// schemes fall through to the generic parse error (with the credential
871		// fragment still redacted by redactURLError) and are then rejected by the
872		// scheme check that already follows url.Parse.
873		p := splitUpstream(raw)
874		if scheme := strings.ToLower(raw[:p.schemeEnd]); scheme != "http" && scheme != "https" {
875			return nil
876		}
877		return failuref("invalid_config",
878			"%s: upstream %q contains an invalid percent escape in its userinfo: the username or password before the '@' carries a '%%' that is not followed by two hexadecimal digits, so the address cannot be parsed; write a literal percent as %%25 and percent-encode every other byte as two hex digits. The configured username and password are not repeated — shown together as \"***\" — while the '@', host, port and base path stay unchanged",
879			routeLabel(loc, id), redactUpstreamUserinfo(raw))
880	}

882	func validateUpstream(raw, loc, id string) *Failure {
883		if strings.ContainsAny(raw, "?#") {
884			return failuref("invalid_config", "%s (id %q): upstream must not contain a query string or fragment", loc, id)
885		}
886		// Validate the host's IP-literal spelling against the raw string before
887		// url.Parse: square brackets are the IP-literal marker, so whatever they
888		// enclose must be a legal IPv6 address (full, compressed or IPv4-tail,
889		// zone included) rather than a name or an IPv4 address, and an IPv6
890		// literal may never appear without that pair of brackets. Both checks and
891		// the later join read the same splitUpstream boundaries, which keeps the
892		// rules independent of url.Parse's parser strictness and lets the reason
893		// name the field and the actual problem instead of surfacing a generic URL
894		// parse error (an unbracketed literal otherwise reaches the user as a
895		// misleading "invalid port" complaint).
896		p := splitUpstream(raw)
897		if f := validateBracketedUpstreamHost(p, loc, id); f != nil {
898			return f
899		}
900		if f := validateUnbracketedUpstreamHost(p, loc, id); f != nil {
901			return f
902		}
903		if f := validateUpstreamHostPresent(p, loc, id); f != nil {
904			return f
905		}
906		if f := validateUpstreamPortRange(p, loc, id); f != nil {
907			return f
908		}
909		if f := validateUpstreamBasePathSpace(p, loc, id); f != nil {
910			return f
911		}
912		u, err := url.Parse(raw)
913		if err != nil {
914			if f := invalidUpstreamUserinfoEscape(raw, err, loc, id); f != nil {
915				// A malformed percent escape in the username or password makes
916				// url.Parse quote the credential fragment (e.g. invalid URL
917				// escape "%zz"); replace that whole message with a fixed,
918				// fragment-free reason located on this route and field.
919				return f
920			}
921			return failuref("invalid_config", "%s (id %q): upstream is not a valid URL: %s", loc, id, redactURLError(err))
922		}
923		if u.Scheme != "http" && u.Scheme != "https" {
924			return failuref("invalid_config", "%s (id %q): upstream must be an absolute http or https URL", loc, id)
925		}
926		if u.Host == "" {
927			return failuref("invalid_config", "%s (id %q): upstream must include a host", loc, id)
928		}
929		return nil
930	}

932	// validateUpstreamHostPresent enforces on the split raw boundaries that the
933	// authority carries a non-empty host:
934	//
935	//	scheme "://" [userinfo "@"] host [":" port] [basePath]
936	//
937	// The check is needed because url.Parse treats a leading colon as a port
938	// separator with an empty hostname: it reads "http://:8080/base" with
939	// Host==":8080" and Hostname()=="" instead of rejecting it, so a check on
940	// u.Host alone lets the address through and the joined upstream is emitted
941	// without a host. The raw decision therefore fails every hostPort that is
942	// empty or begins with the port colon — an empty authority
943	// ("http:///base"), an authority reduced to userinfo ("http://u@/base"),
944	// a bare port with or without digits ("http://:8080/base",
945	// "https://:8443", "http://:/base") and any of those after userinfo
946	// ("https://user:p%40ss@:8443/v1"). Neither userinfo, the port nor a base
947	// path can fill the host slot, no default address is ever substituted, and
948	// a host that is simply followed by an empty port ("http://host:/base")
949	// stays accepted: its hostPort begins with the host, not the separator.
950	// Like the bracket rules this is a content error in a syntactically valid
951	// JSON document — the reason names the route's 1-based position, its id and
952	// the upstream field and says the upstream is missing a host, never that
953	// the JSON is broken or that an IPv6 literal needs brackets. The address is
954	// shown with any userinfo hidden (redactUpstreamUserinfo), so the reason
955	// cannot leak the configured credentials into a saved diagnostic.
956	func validateUpstreamHostPresent(p upstreamParts, loc, id string) *Failure {
957		if p.schemeEnd < 0 {
958			return nil // no scheme: the generic absolute-URL check reports this
959		}
960		hostPort := p.hostPort
961		if hostPort != "" && hostPort[0] != ':' {
962			return nil
963		}
964		return failuref("invalid_config",
965			"%s: upstream %q is missing a host: the address must carry a non-empty host before any port (e.g. \"http://example.com:8080/base\"); a port cannot serve as the host, and userinfo or a base path cannot fill the host in either; no default host is added",
966			routeLabel(loc, id), redactUpstreamUserinfo(p.raw))
967	}
968	
969	// validateUpstreamPortRange enforces the TCP port range on an explicitly
970	// written, non-empty, all-digits port in the upstream address:
971	//
972	//	scheme "://" [userinfo "@"] host [":" port] [basePath]
973	//
974	// A port is a decimal number from 0 to 65535, both ends included; 65536 or
975	// anything larger is not a TCP port and the whole configuration fails as
976	// invalid_config. The decision is made on the decimal value, not the string
977	// length: leading zeros change nothing ("00065535" is legal, "00065536" is
978	// not), and the digit string is compared without ever being converted to an
979	// integer, so a port of arbitrary length cannot overflow a conversion into
980	// an accepted value or crash the read. The comparison is length-then-
981	// lexicographic against "65535" on the zero-stripped digits, which is exact
982	// for equal-length decimal strings.
983	//
984	// The port is sliced out of the same splitUpstream hostPort boundaries the
985	// host validators and the final join use, so only the real port is judged:
986	// the colon inside userinfo ends at the last '@' before hostPort is even
987	// formed, the colons of an IPv6 literal sit inside the bracket pair the
988	// bracketed-host check already validated (its port is the digits after the
989	// closing ']'), and a number in the base path is past the first path slash
990	// and never reaches hostPort. Ordinary domains, bare IPv4 hosts and
991	// bracketed IPv6 hosts all answer to the same range.
992	//
993	// Only an explicitly written non-empty digit run is judged here: an absent
994	// port and the existing legal "host:" spelling (a colon with an empty port)
995	// stay accepted, and port text that is not all digits keeps its existing
996	// owner — the bracketed-host shape check for a bracketed host, the generic
997	// URL parse error otherwise — so this check never rewords an illegal-port
998	// error that already exists. The check runs in check layer 4
999	// (Config.validate) after the host-shape rules, in routes-array order like
1000	// the other field-content checks, so every earlier error keeps its
1001	// precedence and one bad route fails the whole read even when a request
1002	// would only have hit another, legal route. The reason names the route's
1003	// 1-based position, its id and the upstream field and says the port is
1004	// outside 0–65535; this is a content error in a syntactically valid JSON
1005	// document, never a JSON parse failure. A legal port is never normalized:
1006	// the join slices the raw upstream, so "00065535" reaches upstreamURL with
1007	// its leading zeros intact.
1008	func validateUpstreamPortRange(p upstreamParts, loc, id string) *Failure {
1009		if p.schemeEnd < 0 {
1010			return nil // no scheme: the generic absolute-URL check reports this
1011		}
1012		port, ok := upstreamExplicitPort(p.hostPort)
1013		if !ok || port == "" {
1014			return nil
1015		}
1016		for i := 0; i < len(port); i++ {
1017			if port[i] < '0' || port[i] > '9' {
1018				// Not a numeric port: the existing illegal-port checks own it.
1019				return nil
1020			}
1021		}
1022		if portWithinTCPRange(port) {
1023			return nil
1024		}
1025		return failuref("invalid_config",
1026			"%s: upstream port %q is out of range: an explicitly written port must be a decimal number from 0 to 65535 (leading zeros do not change the value); the address is used exactly as configured and the port is never clamped, truncated or rewritten",
1027			routeLabel(loc, id), port)
1028	}
1029	
1030	// upstreamExplicitPort slices the explicitly written port out of a hostPort
1031	// (the authority after the last '@', per splitUpstream). It reports false
1032	// when there is no port separator at all; a present separator with an empty
1033	// port ("host:") reports the empty string with true, and the caller leaves
1034	// that existing legal spelling alone. The shape decisions of the host
1035	// validators are trusted, not repeated: a bracketed host's port follows the
1036	// closing ']', and an unbracketed hostPort carries at most one colon — the
1037	// one separating host and port — because validateUnbracketedUpstreamHost
1038	// already rejected anything with more.
1039	func upstreamExplicitPort(hostPort string) (port string, ok bool) {
1040		if hostPort == "" {
1041			return "", false
1042		}
1043		if hostPort[0] == '[' {
1044			closeBracket := strings.IndexByte(hostPort, ']')
1045			if closeBracket < 0 {
1046				return "", false // owned by the bracketed-host check
1047			}
1048			suffix := hostPort[closeBracket+1:]
1049			if suffix == "" || suffix[0] != ':' {
1050				return "", false
1051			}
1052			return suffix[1:], true
1053		}
1054		if strings.Count(hostPort, ":") != 1 {
1055			return "", false
1056		}
1057		return hostPort[strings.IndexByte(hostPort, ':')+1:], true
1058	}
1059	
1060	// portWithinTCPRange reports whether an all-digits port string names a value
1061	// from 0 to 65535 inclusive. The digits are never converted to an integer:
1062	// leading zeros are stripped and the remaining string is compared against
1063	// "65535" by length and then lexicographically, which decides the decimal
1064	// order exactly and cannot overflow no matter how long the input is. An
1065	// all-zeros port strips to the empty string and is in range (it is 0).
1066	func portWithinTCPRange(port string) bool {
1067		trimmed := strings.TrimLeft(port, "0")
1068		if len(trimmed) > len("65535") {
1069			return false
1070		}
1071		return len(trimmed) < len("65535") || trimmed <= "65535"
1072	}
1073	
1074	// validateUpstreamBasePathSpace rejects a direct ASCII space (U+0020) in the
1075	// upstream base path — inside a path segment, beside a slash or at the end,
1076	// it is all the same error. Only percent encoding may carry a space there:
1077	// "%20" is legal path content and is never decoded first, so an encoded
1078	// space stays accepted while the literal byte is rejected. The check reads
1079	// the same splitUpstream base-path boundaries the join uses, so a space that
1080	// would reach upstreamURL can never pass validation. It is decided on the
1081	// decoded configured string (a " " JSON escape decodes to the same
1082	// byte), only the ASCII space is rejected — the rule is not widened to other
1083	// Unicode whitespace — and the address is judged exactly as configured: the
1084	// space is never stripped, the path never trimmed and the byte never
1085	// re-encoded on the user's behalf. The reason names the route's 1-based
1086	// position, its id and the upstream field; like the host rules this is a
1087	// content error in a syntactically valid JSON document, never a JSON parse
1088	// failure.
1089	func validateUpstreamBasePathSpace(p upstreamParts, loc, id string) *Failure {
1090		if p.schemeEnd < 0 {
1091			return nil // no scheme: the generic absolute-URL check reports this
1092		}
1093		if !strings.ContainsRune(p.basePath, ' ') {
1094			return nil
1095		}
1096		return failuref("invalid_config",
1097			"%s: upstream base path contains an unencoded space (U+0020): a space in the upstream address must be percent-encoded as %%20 in the configuration; the address is used exactly as configured and the space is never stripped, the path never trimmed and the byte never encoded on its behalf",
1098			routeLabel(loc, id))
1099	}
1100	
1101	// validateBracketedUpstreamHost checks the split raw upstream's authority for
1102	// an IP literal in square brackets: brackets are reserved for an IPv6 (or
1103	// future IP-version) literal, so their content must parse as an IPv6 address
1104	// — full form, compressed form or an IPv6 address with an embedded IPv4
1105	// tail — and the brackets must wrap the whole host exactly once:
1106	//
1107	//	"[" IPv6 "]" [ ":" *DIGIT ]
1108	//
1109	// A port, userinfo and a percent-encoded zone ("%25eth0") are allowed and
1110	// never alter the literal's bytes; an empty pair of brackets, a plain
1111	// hostname such as "[not-an-ip]", a bare IPv4 address such as
1112	// "[127.0.0.1]", a malformed IPv6 literal, a missing closing bracket, a
1113	// second bracket group such as "[::1][::2]", a stray closing bracket or any
1114	// other text between the closing bracket and the start of the base path
1115	// (including junk around the port such as "[::1]:80a" or "[::1]x]:80") are
1116	// rejected — a legal first literal never legitimizes trailing content. The
1117	// reason names the route, its id and the upstream field. This is a content
1118	// error in a syntactically valid JSON document, never a JSON parse failure,
1119	// and the rule is enforced here on the raw bytes rather than left to
1120	// url.Parse's parser strictness.
1121	func validateBracketedUpstreamHost(p upstreamParts, loc, id string) *Failure {
1122		if p.schemeEnd < 0 {
1123			return nil // no scheme: the generic absolute-URL check reports this
1124		}
1125		hostPort := p.hostPort
1126	
1127		if !strings.ContainsAny(hostPort, "[]") {
1128			return nil // ordinary reg-name (domain) or bare IPv4 host stays as-is
1129		}
1130		label := routeLabel(loc, id)
1131		if !strings.HasPrefix(hostPort, "[") {
1132			return failuref("invalid_config",
1133				"%s: upstream bracketed host must be a single '[' IPv6 address ']' pair: '[' may only open the host", label)
1134		}
1135		closeBracket := strings.IndexByte(hostPort, ']')
1136		if closeBracket < 0 {
1137			return failuref("invalid_config",
1138				"%s: upstream bracketed host must be a valid IPv6 address but the closing ']' is missing", label)
1139		}
1140		literal := hostPort[1:closeBracket]
1141		// The zone delimiter is percent-encoded in the URL ("%25"); decode the
1142		// literal's escapes once so netip sees "fe80::1%eth0" while every other
1143		// byte keeps its original spelling.
1144		decoded, err := url.PathUnescape(literal)
1145		if err != nil {
1146			return invalidBracketedHost(label, literal)
1147		}
1148		addr, err := netip.ParseAddr(decoded)
1149		if err != nil || !addr.Is6() {
1150			// ParseAddr accepts a bare IPv4 address; brackets may only carry
1151			// IPv6, so "[127.0.0.1]" is rejected even though it is a valid IP.
1152			return invalidBracketedHost(label, literal)
1153		}
1154		// The one closing bracket ends the host: the rest of the authority may
1155		// be empty or the optional port the generic parser already allows
1156		// (":" followed by digits, an empty port included). A repeated bracket
1157		// group, a stray ']', or any other text before, beside or after a port
1158		// fails here even though the first literal was valid — the brackets
1159		// must enclose the whole host exactly once.
1160		suffix := hostPort[closeBracket+1:]
1161		switch {
1162		case suffix == "":
1163			return nil
1164		case strings.ContainsAny(suffix, "[]"):
1165			return invalidBracketedHostShape(label, suffix)
1166		case suffix[0] != ':':
1167			return invalidBracketedHostShape(label, suffix)
1168		}
1169		port := suffix[1:]
1170		for i := 0; i < len(port); i++ {
1171			if port[i] < '0' || port[i] > '9' {
1172				return invalidBracketedHostShape(label, suffix)
1173			}
1174		}
1175		return nil
1176	}

1178	// invalidBracketedHost builds the content error for a bracketed host whose

1182			"%s: upstream host in brackets must be a valid IPv6 address, but %q is not a legal IPv6 address", label, literal)

1185	// validateUnbracketedUpstreamHost checks the split raw upstream's
1186	// authority-without-brackets (hostPort) against the authority grammar:
1187	//
1188	//	host = IP-literal / IPv4address / reg-name
1189	//	IP-literal = "[" ( IPv6address / ... ) "]"
1190	//
1191	// An unbracketed host part may therefore carry at most one colon, the one
1192	// separating the host from its port:
1193	//
1194	//	reg-name [ ":" port ]
1195	//
1196	// Two or more colons are illegal no matter what the bytes spell: a bare IPv6
1197	// literal leaves the host/port boundary undefined (the reader cannot tell
1198	// "::1" from "::1:8080" with a port) and must be written as "[2001:db8::1]",
1199	// while a name such as "api:internal:8080" or even a malformed IPv6-shaped
1200	// spelling such as "2001:db8:::1" is not rescued by a numeric last segment —
1201	// an extra colon stays an extra colon whether or not the address parses as
1202	// IPv6 and whether or not a base path follows. The spelling is rejected on
1203	// the colon count alone: the host and port are never guessed apart, brackets
1204	// are never inserted and a trailing run of digits is never promoted to a
1205	// port, so validity never depends on this Go release's url.Parse port
1206	// strictness.
1207	//
1208	// When the part does parse as an IPv6 literal as written, the reason keeps
1209	// the existing missing-brackets wording; a part that is merely
1210	// multi-colon gets the extra-colon wording. The decision never strips a
1211	// trailing ":<digits>" segment as a hypothetical port: every true bare IPv6
1212	// spelling already parses whole ("::1:8080" and "fe80::1:8443" are complete
1213	// addresses, whose last hextet merely happens to be digits), so stripping
1214	// would only mislabel a malformed spelling such as "2001:db8:::1" that
1215	// parses once a hextet is removed. Both reasons cover every form — the full
1216	// form, the compressed form ("::1"), an IPv6 address with an embedded IPv4
1217	// tail ("::ffff:192.0.2.1") and a percent-encoded zone ("%25eth0") — and
1218	// both name the route's 1-based position, its id and the upstream field.
1219	//
1220	// Ordinary domains and bare IPv4 hosts (with or without a port) stay
1221	// untouched, and the colons in userinfo or the base path are never
1222	// inspected: only hostPort — the authority after the last '@' and before
1223	// the first '/' according to the shared splitUpstream boundaries — is
1224	// considered. Like the bracketed-host rule this is a content error in a
1225	// syntactically valid JSON document, never a JSON parse failure, and it is
1226	// decided on the raw bytes before url.Parse so the wording cannot regress to
1227	// that parser's generic "invalid port" error. When the reason quotes the
1228	// whole address, any userinfo is hidden first (redactUpstreamUserinfo), so
1229	// the diagnostic cannot leak the configured credentials.
1230	func validateUnbracketedUpstreamHost(p upstreamParts, loc, id string) *Failure {
1231		if p.schemeEnd < 0 {
1232			return nil // no scheme: the generic absolute-URL check reports this
1233		}
1234		hostPort := p.hostPort
1235		if hostPort == "" || strings.ContainsAny(hostPort, "[]") {
1236			// No host (the generic check reports it) or a bracketed literal,
1237			// which the bracketed-host validator owns.
1238			return nil
1239		}
1240	
1241		// A single colon is the legal host/port separator ("host:8080"); zero
1242		// colons is a bare host. Count raw colons only: percent-encoded colons
1243		// ("%3A") carry no separator byte, and userinfo and the base path were
1244		// sliced off by splitUpstream.
1245		if strings.Count(hostPort, ":") <= 1 {
1246			return nil
1247		}
1248		label := routeLabel(loc, id)
1249	
1250		// Classify the spelling as written, never guessing a host/port split:
1251		// percent-decode once so a "%25eth0" zone reaches netip as "%eth0" while
1252		// every other byte keeps its spelling, then parse the whole hostPort. A
1253		// legal IPv6 literal keeps the existing missing-brackets reason (this
1254		// covers every form, "::1:8080" and "fe80::1:8443" included — a trailing
1255		// hextet of digits is part of the address, not a guessed port); anything
1256		// else that merely carries extra colons gets the extra-colon reason.
1257		decoded, err := url.PathUnescape(hostPort)
1258		if err == nil {
1259			if addr, perr := netip.ParseAddr(decoded); perr == nil && addr.Is6() {
1260				return failuref("invalid_config",
1261					"%s: upstream IPv6 host %q is missing its square brackets: an IPv6 literal must be enclosed in a pair of brackets with any port outside them (e.g. \"[2001:db8::1]:8080\"); brackets are never added and a trailing number is not guessed as a port",
1262					label, hostPort)
1263			}
1264		}
1265		return failuref("invalid_config",
1266			"%s: upstream %q has an unbracketed host part %q with more than one colon: a host without square brackets may contain at most the one colon separating it from its port (e.g. \"example.com:8080\"); an IPv6 literal must be enclosed in brackets (e.g. \"[2001:db8::1]:8080\") and the host and port are never guessed apart",
1267			label, redactUpstreamUserinfo(p.raw), hostPort)
1268	}

1279	// requestJSON mirrors Request but keeps method and target raw, so a valid
1280	// JSON document whose fields merely have the wrong JSON type is reported on
1281	// the offending field instead of as a generic JSON decode error.
1282	type requestJSON struct {
1283		Method json.RawMessage `json:"method"`
1284		Target json.RawMessage `json:"target"`
1285	}

1287	// ParseRequest parses and validates one JSON request. Three failure shapes are
1288	// kept apart: a document whose JSON syntax is broken fails as a parse failure
1289	// without guessing a field; a syntactically valid non-object document (array,
1290	// number, string, boolean or null) must be a JSON object; a valid object whose
1291	// method or target is not a string fails on that field, naming the JSON type
1292	// actually received (null counts as a type error, never as a missing field).
1293	// method is always checked before target, regardless of the key order in the
1294	// object. Only after both fields are present strings are their contents
1295	// (required method, legal token, absolute target without a fragment, a bad
1296	// percent escape, or a direct space/control character) validated, so an empty
1297	// string stays a content error.
1298	func ParseRequest(data []byte) (*Request, *Failure) {
1299		body, err := unmarshalJSONValue(data)
1300		if err != nil {
1301			return nil, failuref("invalid_request", "request is not valid JSON: %v", err)
1302		}
1303		if f := requireJSONObject(body, "invalid_request", "request", false); f != nil {
1304			return nil, f
1305		}
1306	
1307		var rj requestJSON
1308		if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &rj); err != nil {
1309			// The document already parsed as one JSON value and starts with '{';
1310			// keep this as a parse failure rather than a field error if the object
1311			// itself cannot be read.
1312			return nil, failuref("invalid_request", "request is not valid JSON: %v", err)
1313		}
1314	
1315		var req Request
1316		// method is always checked before target, regardless of the key order in
1317		// the object; the absent/null/non-string distinction is the shared
1318		// decodeStringField, so only the request wording is added here.
1319		if f := decodeRequestStringField(rj.Method, "method", &req.Method); f != nil {
1320			return nil, f
1321		}
1322		if f := decodeRequestStringField(rj.Target, "target", &req.Target); f != nil {
1323			return nil, f
1324		}
1325	
1326		switch {
1327		case req.Method == "":
1328			return nil, failuref("invalid_request", "method is required")
1329		case !isToken(req.Method):
1330			return nil, failuref("invalid_request", "method %q is not a legal HTTP method", req.Method)
1331		}
1332		switch {
1333		case req.Target == "" || req.Target[0] != '/':
1334			return nil, failuref("invalid_request", "target must start with /")
1335		case strings.Contains(req.Target, "#"):
1336			return nil, failuref("invalid_request", "target must not contain a fragment")
1337		case !validPercentEscapes(req.Target):
1338			return nil, failuref("invalid_request", "target contains an invalid percent escape")
1339		}
1340		if f := validateTargetCharacters(req.Target); f != nil {
1341			return nil, f
1342		}
1343		return &req, nil
1344	}
1345	
1346	// decodeRequestStringField renders the request wording for one string field;
1347	// the absent/null/non-string decision itself is the shared
1348	// decodeStringField. An absent field (no such key) is left as the zero value
1349	// so the later content checks keep their "field is required" behavior; null
1350	// or any non-string JSON value is a type error that names the field and the
1351	// JSON type that was actually supplied.
1352	func decodeRequestStringField(raw json.RawMessage, field string, dst *string) *Failure {
1353		if !decodeStringField(raw, dst) {
1354			return failuref("invalid_request", "%s must be a string, got %s", field, jsonTypeName(raw))
1355		}
1356		return nil
1357	}

1359	// jsonTypeName names the JSON type of a syntactically valid raw value, in the
1360	// terms the request error reasons use: "null", "a boolean", "a number",
1361	// "a string", "an array" or "an object".
1362	func jsonTypeName(raw json.RawMessage) string {
1363		switch bytes.TrimSpace(raw)[0] {
1364		case 'n':
1365			return "null"
1366		case 't', 'f':
1367			return "a boolean"
1368		case '"':
1369			return "a string"
1370		case '[':
1371			return "an array"
1372		case '{':
1373			return "an object"
1374		default:
1375			return "a number"
1376		}
1377	}

1379	// Resolve matches a validated request against a validated configuration and
1380	// computes the upstream URL. Failure codes are route_not_found and
1381	// route_conflict.
1382	func Resolve(cfg *Config, req *Request) (*Resolution, *Failure) {
1383		// Reject a target carrying a direct space or control character before
1384		// route selection, conflict resolution and query rewriting, so such a
1385		// request can never match a prefix (and carry the byte into
1386		// upstreamURL), report a conflict, or have a remove/set hide the
1387		// offending parameter. ParseRequest already ran this check; it is
1388		// repeated here so a request built in-process cannot bypass it.
1389		if f := validateTargetCharacters(req.Target); f != nil {
1390			return nil, f
1391		}
1392		path := req.Target
1393		if i := strings.IndexByte(path, '?'); i >= 0 {
1394			path = path[:i]
1395		}
1396	
1397		type candidate struct {
1398			route    *Route
1399			concrete bool
1400		}
1401		var matched []candidate
1402		for i := range cfg.Routes {
1403			route := &cfg.Routes[i]
1404			concrete, wildcard := methodMatch(route.Methods, req.Method)
1405			if !concrete && !wildcard {
1406				continue
1407			}
1408			if !prefixMatch(route.PathPrefix, path) {
1409				continue
1410			}
1411			matched = append(matched, candidate{route, concrete})
1412		}
1413		if len(matched) == 0 {
1414			return nil, failuref("route_not_found", "no route matches %s %s", req.Method, path)
1415		}
1416	
1417		// Longest prefix wins.
1418		bestLen := 0
1419		for _, c := range matched {
1420			if n := len(c.route.PathPrefix); n > bestLen {
1421				bestLen = n
1422			}
1423		}
1424		winners := matched[:0]
1425		for _, c := range matched {
1426			if len(c.route.PathPrefix) == bestLen {
1427				winners = append(winners, c)
1428			}
1429		}
1430	
1431		// Among equal prefixes a concrete method beats the wildcard.
1432		var concrete []candidate
1433		for _, c := range winners {
1434			if c.concrete {
1435				concrete = append(concrete, c)
1436			}
1437		}
1438		if len(concrete) > 0 {
1439			winners = concrete
1440		}
1441		if len(winners) > 1 {
1442			ids := make([]string, 0, len(winners))
1443			for _, c := range winners {
1444				ids = append(ids, c.route.ID)
1445			}
1446			sort.Strings(ids)
1447			f := failuref("route_conflict", "multiple routes match %s %s", req.Method, path)
1448			f.Candidates = ids
1449			return nil, f
1450		}
1451	
1452		upstreamURL, f := joinUpstream(winners[0].route, path, req.Target)
1453		if f != nil {
1454			return nil, f
1455		}
1456		return &Resolution{RouteID: winners[0].route.ID, UpstreamURL: upstreamURL}, nil
1457	}

1459	// methodMatch reports whether the method list matches the request method
1460	// concretely (an exact, case-sensitive entry) or via the "*" wildcard.
1461	func methodMatch(methods []string, method string) (concrete, wildcard bool) {
1462		for _, m := range methods {
1463			switch {
1464			case m == "*":
1465				wildcard = true
1466			case m == method:
1467				concrete = true
1468			}
1469		}
1470		return concrete, wildcard
1471	}

1473	// prefixMatch matches raw encoded paths on segment boundaries: "%2F" is never
1474	// treated as a separator and the root prefix matches every origin-path.
1475	func prefixMatch(prefix, path string) bool {
1476		if prefix == "/" {
1477			return true
1478		}
1479		if path == prefix {
1480			return true
1481		}
1482		return strings.HasPrefix(path, prefix) && path[len(prefix)] == '/'
1483	}

1485	// joinUpstream strips the route prefix from the request path and joins the
1486	// remainder onto the upstream base path with exactly one slash at the
1487	// junction. The junction is one run of literal slashes: every trailing
1488	// slash on the base path and every leading slash on the remainder are
1489	// merged into that single slash, even when either side contributes
1490	// several. Nothing else is normalized: slashes inside either part, the
1491	// remainder's trailing slashes (once non-slash content has appeared),
1492	// ".", ".." and percent escapes such as "%2F" are carried over byte for
1493	// byte, never decoded first. The base path is sliced out of the raw
1494	// upstream so joining never re-encodes, reorders or drops anything
1495	// outside the junction. The raw query is preserved verbatim unless the
1496	// route defines queryTransforms, in which case they rewrite it after
1497	// route selection.
1498	func joinUpstream(route *Route, path, target string) (string, *Failure) {
1499		if _, err := url.Parse(route.Upstream); err != nil {
1500			// Config validation already rejected this. The parse error is
1501			// rendered with any userinfo hidden, so the fallback reason cannot
1502			// repeat the address with its credentials.
1503			return "", failuref("invalid_config", "route %q has an invalid upstream: %s", route.ID, redactURLError(err))
1504		}
1505	
1506		var remainder string
1507		switch {
1508		case route.PathPrefix == "/":
1509			// Root keeps the whole following path; "/" itself has an empty remainder.
1510			if path != "/" {
1511				remainder = path
1512			}
1513		default:
1514			remainder = path[len(route.PathPrefix):] // "" or "/...", boundary is a literal slash
1515		}
1516	
1517		// Slice the validated upstream raw so nothing outside the junction is
1518		// normalized or re-escaped. The address boundaries come from the same
1519		// splitUpstream reading the host validators used (scheme://authority
1520		// followed by the base path), so joining can never split userinfo, the
1521		// IPv6 brackets, the port or the base path differently than validation.
1522		parts := splitUpstream(route.Upstream)
1523		basePath := parts.basePath
1524	
1525		// Collapse only the junction run: all trailing slashes of the base
1526		// path meet all leading slashes of the remainder, and the junction
1527		// keeps exactly one slash whether or not anything follows them. A
1528		// remainder made entirely of slashes has no content past the run, so
1529		// it likewise ends in that single slash.
1530		baseTrimmed := strings.TrimRight(basePath, "/")
1531		rest := strings.TrimLeft(remainder, "/")
1532		joined := baseTrimmed + "/" + rest
1533	
1534		result := route.Upstream[:parts.schemeEnd+3] + parts.authority + joined
1535		query, f := applyQueryTransforms(route.QueryTransforms, target)
1536		if f != nil {
1537			return "", f
1538		}
1539		return result + query, nil
1540	}

1542	// firstDirectRawCharacter scans raw path text as written — without decoding
1543	// percent escapes — and returns the first byte that may not appear directly:
1544	// an ASCII space (U+0020), a C0 control byte (U+0000 through U+001F) or DEL
1545	// (U+007F). Bytes inside a well-formed percent escape ("%" plus two hex
1546	// digits) are skipped, so "%20", "%0A" and "%09" keep parsing and matching
1547	// on the raw encoded form and never register as a direct character; the
1548	// scan never decodes an escape first. A lone or malformed "%" is traversed
1549	// byte by byte here — such an escape is owned by validPercentEscapes, which
1550	// runs before this scan in both readers, and must not let a following
1551	// offending byte be jumped over. It is the one shared decision of the
1552	// request target rule and the route pathPrefix rule, so the two sides that
1553	// must agree on which bytes may appear directly cannot drift apart.
1554	func firstDirectRawCharacter(s string) (byte, bool) {
1555		for i := 0; i < len(s); i++ {
1556			c := s[i]
1557			if c == '%' && i+2 < len(s) && isHex(s[i+1]) && isHex(s[i+2]) {
1558				i += 2
1559				continue
1560			}
1561			if c == ' ' || c < 0x20 || c == 0x7f {
1562				return c, true
1563			}
1564		}
1565		return 0, false
1566	}
1567	
1568	// validateTargetCharacters enforces on the raw target that only percent
1569	// encoding may carry a space or a control character: a direct ASCII space
1570	// (U+0020), a C0 control byte (U+0000 through U+001F) or DEL (U+007F) is
1571	// rejected no matter whether it sits in the path, a parameter name or a
1572	// parameter value. Invalid percent escapes are owned by
1573	// validPercentEscapes, which runs before this check, so a lone or malformed
1574	// "%" keeps its existing reason. The reason names the first offending
1575	// character as U+XXXX.
1576	func validateTargetCharacters(target string) *Failure {
1577		if c, ok := firstDirectRawCharacter(target); ok {
1578			return failuref("invalid_request",
1579				"target contains a character that must be percent-encoded: U+%04X is not allowed to appear directly (percent-encode it, e.g. %%20 for a space)",
1580				c)
1581		}
1582		return nil
1583	}

1585	// isToken reports whether s is an RFC 7230 token, i.e. a legal HTTP method.
1586	func isToken(s string) bool {
1587		if s == "" {
1588			return false
1589		}
1590		for i := 0; i < len(s); i++ {
1591			if !isTokenChar(s[i]) {
1592				return false
1593			}
1594		}
1595		return true
1596	}

1598	func isTokenChar(c byte) bool {
1599		switch {
1600		case c >= 'a' && c <= 'z', c >= 'A' && c <= 'Z', c >= '0' && c <= '9':
1601			return true
1602		}
1603		switch c {
1604		case '!', '#', '$', '%', '&', '\'', '*', '+', '-', '.', '^', '_', '`', '|', '~':
1605			return true
1606		}
1607		return false
1608	}

1610	// validPercentEscapes checks that every "%' is followed by two hex digits.
1611	// Matching and joining stay on raw strings, but malformed escapes are rejected
1612	// up front for both prefixes and request targets.
1613	func validPercentEscapes(s string) bool {
1614		for i := 0; i < len(s); i++ {
1615			if s[i] != '%' {
1616				continue
1617			}
1618			if i+2 >= len(s) || !isHex(s[i+1]) || !isHex(s[i+2]) {
1619				return false
1620			}
1621			i += 2
1622		}
1623		return true
1624	}
1625	
1626	func isHex(c byte) bool {
1627		switch {
1628		case c >= '0' && c <= '9', c >= 'a' && c <= 'f', c >= 'A' && c <= 'F':
1629			return true
1630		}
1631		return false

8	// This file pins, as regression coverage, which error ParseConfig selects and
9	// where it points when several errors coexist in one configuration document.
10	// The rules under test are the existing accept/reject rules; the precedence
11	// they rely on is layered in Config.UnmarshalJSON:
12	//
13	//  1. JSON syntax (a broken document is only ever a parse failure),
14	//  2. the routes element type and the id/methods/pathPrefix/upstream field
15	//     types (type errors),
16	//  3. queryTransforms array and rule validity (rule errors),
17	//  4. field contents such as a non-absolute pathPrefix, a bad method token or
18	//     an empty id (content errors, in Config.validate).
19	//
20	// Within one layer the earliest array position wins: routes by their position
21	// in the routes array and rules by their position in the route's
22	// queryTransforms array, never by id ordering. Every failure must hand back no
23	// config at all, so no half-parsed configuration can ever resolve a request.
24	
25	// expectInvalidConfig parses src and requires an invalid_config Failure whose
26	// reason contains every want substring and none of the forbidden substrings,
27	// and requires ParseConfig to hand back no config. It returns the Failure for
28	// any extra, test-specific assertions.
29	func expectInvalidConfig(t *testing.T, src string, want, forbidden []string) *Failure {
30		t.Helper()
31		cfg, f := ParseConfig([]byte(src))
32		if f == nil {
33			t.Fatalf("expected invalid_config, config was accepted: %s", src)
34		}
35		if f.Code != "invalid_config" {
36			t.Fatalf("code = %q, want invalid_config", f.Code)
37		}
38		if cfg != nil {
39			t.Fatalf("a rejected config must not be returned (no half config to resolve with), got %+v", cfg)
40		}
41		for _, sub := range want {
42			if !strings.Contains(f.Reason, sub) {
43				t.Fatalf("reason = %q, want substring %q\nconfig: %s", f.Reason, sub, src)
44			}
45		}
46		for _, sub := range forbidden {
47			if strings.Contains(f.Reason, sub) {
48				t.Fatalf("reason = %q must not contain %q\nconfig: %s", f.Reason, sub, src)
49			}
50		}
51		return f
52	}

56	// is reported before ANY queryTransforms rule error — even when the rule error
57	// sits on an earlier route. The reported reason targets the offending route's
58	// field, carries that route's valid non-empty id wherever the id appears in
59	// the object, and is independent of the object's field order. The document is
60	// legal JSON, so it must never be described as a parse failure.
